title: No, na, do, da — prepositions that fuse with the article
goal: Master the contractions that have been popping up unexplained since Unit 2, then use them to ask for directions and describe where things are in town.
bekal: fuse *de*, *em*, *a* and *por* with the article without thinking
ask *Onde fica...?* and understand a Portuguese answer
describe location with *ao lado de*, *em frente a*, *entre*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Como se vai para o Rossio?
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost in the Baixa. He asks a woman waiting at a bus stop.

lines.text: Desculpe, onde fica a estação do Rossio?

notes: **Onde fica...? not Onde está...?** For buildings, streets, towns and anything that can't move, the Portuguese use *ficar*. *Onde está a chave?* (a key — it can move) but *Onde fica a estação?* (a station — it isn't going anywhere). Using *estar* for a building isn't wrong, but *ficar* is far more natural.

**A cinco minutos a pé** — notice two different uses of *a* in one short sentence. *A cinco minutos* marks distance ("five minutes away"), *a pé* marks the means ("on foot"). Likewise *de carro* (by car), *de comboio* (by train), but always *a pé* — feet are the only ones that take *a*.
**Comboio, not trem.** A train in Portugal is *o comboio*; in Brazil it's *o trem*. This is one of the vocabulary differences that most often trips up travelers who learned from Brazilian materials.

**Obrigado pela ajuda** — *pela* is *por* fused with *a*. The pattern *obrigado por...* is used to say thanks for something specific: *obrigado pela ajuda*, *obrigado pelo café*, *obrigada pela informação*.
**Está bem** means "all right" or "OK", and you'll hear it constantly. In fast speech it shrinks to *tá bem*, then just *tá* — much like English "OK" becoming "'kay".

grammars.title: Four prepositions that must fuse
body: These contractions **can't be split**. Writing *de o* or *em a* isn't a different style — it's wrong, and it's instantly noticeable.
after: **Notice the ` on à.** It marks that two *a*'s have merged into one, and the sound becomes more open: *à* is said **ah**, while a plain *a* is the short **uh**. This mark is what separates *vou a casa* from *vou à escola*.
*de* also fuses with the indefinite article — *dum*, *duma* — and with third-person pronouns: *dele*, *dela*, *deles*, *delas* (Unit 5). Likewise *em*: *num*, *numa*, *nele*, *nela*.

**These contractions also happen before place names that take an article:** *no Porto*, *no Brasil*, *na Indonésia*, *nos Estados Unidos*. But *em Portugal*, *em Lisboa*, *em Bandung* — because those names take no article. Unfortunately, which ones do and which don't has to be learned one by one.

grammars.title: Prepositions of place
body: Most are compounds ending in *de* or *a* — which means both fuse with the article that follows.
after: **Entre is the only one that doesn't fuse**, because it doesn't end in a preposition. Just *entre o banco e o correio* — the two things joined with *e*.
*Daqui* is *de* fused with *aqui*: "from here". Likewise *dali* (from there), *daí* (from that spot).

blocks.text: **A paragem** is a bus stop in Portugal; in Brazil it's *o ponto*. And *a igreja* has a famous English cousin: both come from Greek *ekklesia*, the source of English *ecclesiastical*.

blocks.title: Getting around in Portugal — and the names that differ from Brazil
items: *o autocarro* (bus) — in Brazil *o ônibus*. *o comboio* (train) — in Brazil *o trem*.
*o elétrico* is the yellow streetcar that's a symbol of Lisbon. *o metro* is the same in both countries.
All vehicles take **de**: *de autocarro*, *de comboio*, *de carro*, *de metro*, *de táxi*. The only exception: *a pé*.
